output.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time when dissemination in space is established by MRI. This permits an MS diagnosis after a single clinical attack (CIS), avoiding the need to wait for a second clinical relapse. DIS requires T2 lesions in at least 2 of 4 characteristic CNS regions. The substitution rule applies only when OCBs are CSF-restricted (absent in paired serum).

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

July 2026 review applied end to end: brain and cervical/thoracic cord MRI use an MS protocol; CSF is conditional, never mandatory; OCT/VEP and AQP4/MOG testing answer selected optic or atypical questions rather than forming a blanket panel.

The 2024 revised McDonald framework recognizes the optic nerve as a fifth topography and accepts the kappa free-light-chain index as an alternative positive-CSF marker; these additions do not make optic testing or lumbar puncture universal.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Amara Osei is a 26-year-old right-handed African American woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a five-day history of progressive vision loss in her left eye accompanied by pain behind the eye that worsens with eye movement. She reports that five days ago she began noticing blurring and fogginess in her left visual field while studying on her laptop, which she initially attributed to eye strain and fatigue. By the following morning the vision had worsened considerably, and she noticed that colors appeared washed out, particularly reds, which looked brownish through the left eye. She also developed a dull aching pain behind the left eye that became sharper with lateral and upward gaze movements, rating it a 6 out of 10 at worst. Over the next three days, the vision in her left eye deteriorated to the point where she could only perceive hand motions centrally, prompting her roommates to bring her to the emergency department. She reports that her symptoms seem to worsen after hot showers, with the vision becoming even more blurred for 30 to 60 minutes after exposure to heat. On further directed questioning, she recalls that approximately eight months ago she had a two-to-three week episode of tingling and numbness involving the right side of her trunk and right arm in a hemibody distribution. She saw her university health center at the time and was told the numbness was likely stress-related; it resolved spontaneously without treatment. She did not seek further evaluation. She denies any prior episodes of vision loss, diplopia, weakness, ataxia, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or speech difficulty. She denies recent fevers, weight loss, rash, oral ulcers, joint pains, or other systemic symptoms. She denies recent viral illness or vaccinations. She has no history of foreign travel. She is currently in her second year of her PhD program and had been under increased academic stress over the past several weeks.
